title: Incorporation of Reporter Genes into Mitochondrial DNA in Budding Yeast
author: Rzepka, Suhm, et al.
materials: For the biolistic transformation, high yield and purity of plasmids pPT24-mtnLuc and pRS315 (used to identify nuclear transformants) are required. We used QIAGEN Plasmid Midi Kit according to the manufacturer’s protocol, but other high yield kits can likely be used as well. In the last step, the plasmids were eluted with 20 μL of sterile deionised H2O to yield a high concentration (around 7–10 μg/μL).

steps.title: Isolate plasmids pPT24-mtnLuc and pRS315
steps.instruction: Obtain high‑yield, high‑purity plasmid DNA using a QIAGEN Plasmid Midi Kit (or equivalent) following the manufacturer’s protocol; elute each plasmid in 20 µL sterile deionised H₂O to achieve ~7–10 µg/µL concentration.

steps.title: Prepare tungsten‑DNA particles
steps.instruction: Create DNA‑coated tungsten particles for biolistic delivery.

substeps.instruction: Mix 50 mg tungsten powder with 1.5 mL 70 % ethanol.
Vortex briefly and incubate at 22 °C for 10 min.
Spin 15 s at 13,000 × g, discard supernatant, and resuspend the pellet in 1.5 mL sterile deionised H₂O.
Spin again 15 s at 13,000 × g, discard supernatant, and resuspend the pellet in sterile 50 % glycerol (16.7 µL glycerol per mg particles).
Store the glycerol‑suspended particles at –20 °C for ≥4 years.

steps.title: Prepare YP stock solution
steps.instruction: Make a 1 L YP medium stock for later use.

substeps.instruction: Dissolve 20 g tryptone/peptone (20 g/L) and 10 g yeast extract (10 g/L) in deionised water up to 1 L.
Autoclave the solution the same day after preparation.
Store the YP stock at 22 °C for long‑term use.
Prepare separate sterile stock solutions of raffinose (20 % w/v), dextrose (40 % w/v) and glycerol (30 % w/v); autoclave each separately before mixing with YP as needed.

steps.title: Make biolistic transformation plates
steps.instruction: Prepare agar plates suitable for biolistic transformation (≈7 plates, 500 mL total).

substeps.instruction: Weigh and add: 15 g agar (30 g/L), 3.35 g yeast nitrogen base (6.7 g/L), 208 mL sorbitol (1 M, 2.4 M stock), 62.5 mL dextrose (40 % w/v, 5 % final), 50 mg adenine (0.1 mg/mL), 10 mg arginine (0.02 mg/mL), 10 mg uracil (0.02 mg/mL), 7.5 mg histidine (0.015 mg/mL), 7.5 mg tryptophan (0.015 mg/mL), 15 mg lysine (0.03 mg/mL), and 229.5 mL water.
Mix agar and the listed amino acids with 218 mL H₂O; mix yeast nitrogen base with 11.5 mL H₂O; place magnetic stirrers in both bottles to aid dissolution.
Autoclave the agar‑amino‑acid solution and the yeast nitrogen base solution separately, then combine them with the remaining components (sorbitol, dextrose, vitamins, etc.).
Pour the medium into 100 mm × 15 mm Petri dishes (the size required for the biolistic chamber).
Allow plates to dry for at least three days before use.

steps.title: Prepare SD‑Leu auxotrophic plates
steps.instruction: Prepare leucine‑deficient selective plates (≈10 plates, 500 mL total).

substeps.instruction: Weigh and add: 10 g agar (20 g/L), 0.85 g yeast nitrogen base (1.7 g/L), 2.5 g ammonium sulfate (5 g/L), 25 mL dextrose (40 % w/v, 2 % final), 10 mg adenine (0.02 mg/mL), 10 mg arginine (0.02 mg/mL), 10 mg uracil (0.02 mg/mL), 7.5 mg histidine (0.015 mg/mL), 7.5 mg tryptophan (0.015 mg/mL), 15 mg lysine (0.03 mg/mL), and 475 mL water.
Mix agar, yeast nitrogen base, ammonium sulfate and all amino acids with the water; use a magnetic stirrer for thorough mixing.
Adjust the pH of the mixture to 5.5 with KOH.
Autoclave the mixture, then cool slightly and add the autoclaved dextrose solution.
Pour into plates and let solidify; prepare at least one day in advance.
Note: Omit or add different amino acids to customize other auxotrophic selection plates.

steps.title: Prepare YPD/YPG plates
steps.instruction: Make rich media plates with either dextrose or glycerol as carbon source (≈10 plates, 500 mL total).

substeps.instruction: Weigh 10 g agar (2 % w/v).
For YPD: use 475 mL YP stock; for YPG: use 466 mL YP stock.
For YPD: add 25 mL dextrose (40 % w/v, 2 % final). For YPG: add 34 mL glycerol (30 % w/v, 2 % final).
Autoclave dextrose and glycerol solutions separately.
Mix agar with 200 mL of the appropriate YP stock and autoclave this mixture.
After cooling, add the remaining YP stock volume and the appropriate carbon‑source solution (dextrose or glycerol).
Pour into plates and allow to solidify.

description: Here we present an approach to incorporate reporter genes into mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) of budding yeast. Originally, a method was developed in the laboratory of Tom Fox to integrate a reporter gene into a certain open reading frame of the mitochondrial genome (Steele et al., 1996). For this, yeast cells were transformed with a biolistic gene delivery system, followed by screening for a reporter activity. The exchange of an authentic open reading frame to that of the reporter caused inability to perform oxidative phosphorylation with consequences for cellular physiology. Later, the Tom Fox group developed a plasmid, pPT24, which allowed to express a recoded open reading frame in mitochondria as additional gene (Mireau et al., 2003; Thorsness and Fox, 1993). The principle of the latter approach is to incorporate the reporter gene in an otherwise silent region of the mtDNA (Figure 1A). For this, plasmid pPT24 has a unique EcoRI site that allows to clone in a fully functional gene, encompassing a standard promoter driving the expression of an mRNA containing the 5′-untranslated regions (UTRs) of COX2 (Gruschke et al., 2012). Moreover, the plasmid contains a large portion of the upstream region of COX2 including its open reading frame.Figure 1Integration of mtnluc into mitochondria genome(A) Schematic of the plasmid pPT24-mtnLuc that contains mtnuc sequence flanked by COX2 UTRs cloned into the pPT24 plasmid using EcoRI restriction digestion site.(B) Schematic representation of mtnluc integration into mitochondrial genome via homologous recombination. In order to be functionally expressed, the reporter gene needs to be recoded to fit the mitochondrial codon usage and cloned into pPT24. The final plasmid is then delivered into the mitochondria via biolistic transformation where it can finally be recombined with a mutant mtDNA that carries a deletion in the COX2 gene (Figure 1B).
